response.reasoning: The seven members are internally coherent in a way the controls are not: every one consumed zero parts and closed as RESET / NO-FAULT-FOUND / ESCALATED (WO-2025-00449, WO-2025-00612, WO-2025-00651, WO-2025-00813, WO-2025-00847, WO-2026-00627), four explicitly record a *second* overtemp on the same asset in one season (WO-2025-00248, WO-2025-00813, WO-2025-00847, WO-2026-00627), and intakes/filters/heat sinks were recorded clear in every case where they were checked — with two independent hints at the control path (fan 'ramping late' in WO-2025-00248, 'fw 4.2.1' in WO-2025-00847). That pattern of recurring, hardware-negative resets is what a late-ramping thermal-control build looks like, and it is distinguishable from the genuine cooling-hardware failures in the control set, which did consume parts and did resolve (fan seized and replaced, WO-2025-00789; three cooling fans and an open OEM case for afternoon derate, WO-2025-00908) — so this is not simply H4 wear. H2 is weak because the events sit on seven distinct dates across four months and two calendar years and across five sites (Vireo Valley, Sandhill Bend, Tidemarsh Bay, Almond Row, Pecan Fork), not on a handful of heat days. H3 has real force — the narratives in WO-2025-00612, WO-2025-00651 and WO-2025-00449 are near-verbatim, TECH-0051 authored three members, lift is null against a 0.0 peer median, and the whole cluster is 29.3 labor hours and ~3.5 MWh across two seasons — which is exactly why this is real but not worth a campaign. All seven member serials fall in the 2024 manufacture band (weeks 18-35 if the serial encodes YYWW), while none of the older KVP-3600 controls (1813A, 1927C x2) produced an overtemp trip, which is the one thread worth pulling at desk cost.
response.contradicting_evidence: Three member narratives are near-verbatim duplicates and TECH-0051 authored three of seven, so part of the apparent similarity is reporting template rather than independent observation; peer median of 0.0 makes the lift uncomputable, so no true outlier status is demonstrated. Two KVP-3600 controls fall inside the same 2024 manufacture window with no overtemp trip (WO-2025-00614 on 2423B, WO-2025-00908 on 2428C), weakening a tight build-window claim. Firmware version is recorded on exactly one unit (WO-2025-00847), so the central mechanism of H1 rests on a single data point plus one tech's hunch.

response.business_headline: Seven KVP-3600 overtemperature trips cleared by reset with zero parts and four confirmed repeats point to a fan-control firmware behaviour rather than hardware, but at 29.3 labor hours and ~3.5 MWh across two seasons this is a desk-level OEM question to fold into an existing warranty case, not a field campaign.

response.reasoning: Every one of the 6 distinct failing assets carries a 24xx serial prefix (2419B-0365, 2423B-0265, 2428C-0169, 2428C-0165, 2432C-0357, 2434C-0084), i.e. 2024-manufacture units, which are only ~179 of the 376 installed KVP-3600s — and the failures are physical, not just textual (IGBT modules and gate drivers consumed in WO-2026-00480, WO-2026-00696, WO-2026-00702, WO-2026-00595). H2 (discrete 2026 heat episode) is weakened because the matched controls show the same thermal family of events on 2024-build units outside the May–June 2026 window and at other sites: WO-2025-00612 (2432C, Jul 2025 overtemp), WO-2025-00847 (2419B, second overtemp of the season, fw 4.2.1), WO-2026-00627 (2422B, second overtemp this season), while the older-build controls (16xx/18xx: WO-2026-00111, WO-2026-00365, WO-2025-00336) show non-thermal or routine findings. H4 (end-of-life wear) fails on direction — the failing population is the newest cohort in the fleet, not the oldest. H3 has real force and is why confidence is only medium: three near-identical boilerplate narratives, follow-up visits double-counted (2428C-0169 in WO-2026-00522 and WO-2026-00575; 2419B-0365 in WO-2026-00480 and WO-2026-00579, so 6 distinct assets not 8), and parts/resolution fields that contradict the text (WO-2026-00522 lists DC contactors against an IGBT narrative; WO-2026-00575 is PART-REPL with no parts; WO-2026-00514 is CLEANED with a gate driver consumed) — but the coding noise does not explain why the thermal-family events land almost exclusively on the 2024 build cohort, and controls WO-2026-00111 and WO-2025-00665 show that identical IGBT failures get coded 'failure_to_start' elsewhere, meaning the true 2024-cohort event count is likely understated rather than inflated.
response.contradicting_evidence: The cluster is inflated by follow-up chains and boilerplate: 8 work orders resolve to 6 distinct assets (WO-2026-00522/WO-2026-00575 and WO-2026-00480/WO-2026-00579 are pairs on the same asset), dropping the per-unit rate to ~0.016. Serial prefixes span 2024 weeks 19 through 34 rather than a tight build lot, and 2024 units are ~48% of the fleet, so 6/6 from that cohort is suggestive but not decisive at this n. No peer-model work orders were provided in the control set — every control is another KVP-3600 — so the peer_median_rate of 0.0 and the null lift remain unverified, and the tight May-11-to-Jun-30 window is still fully consistent with H2. Firmware 4.2.1 appears on a control asset too (WO-2025-00847, WO-2024-00195), so firmware alone does not separate members from controls.

response.business_headline: Power-stage thermal failures on KVP-3600 inverters are landing exclusively on the 2024-build cohort (179 of 376 units, ~61 labour hours and multiple IGBT/gate-driver swaps in seven weeks) while older builds show none — worth an OEM engineering review and warranty preservation now, not after next summer.

response.reasoning: H2 (text artifact) does not survive the control set: the controls are templated in exactly the same way — WO-2025-00179 and WO-2026-00286 are near-identical overcurrent narratives, and WO-2025-00770 and WO-2025-00465 are near-identical undervoltage narratives — so verbatim phrasing is a corpus-wide narration habit, not evidence that these seven events are one event double-counted; the members carry six distinct asset IDs across four sites and three summers, so they are distinct physical events. H4 is weakened because one member sits at coastal Tidemarsh Bay (WO-2025-00720), not only at the desert sites. What the members actually describe, however, is textbook designed high-ambient protection: a tightly clustered 10-12% afternoon limit, no stored fault and nothing to reset (WO-2025-00670), and the fullest inspection in the set found filters, intake screens and plenum clear with all six fans turning and cabinet temperature recovering after sundown unaided (WO-2026-00586) — H3's signature. H1 cannot be excluded (KVP36-2419B-0361 recurred in WO-2024-00163 and WO-2025-00688, and fans/filters were consumed in WO-2025-00908 and WO-2026-00571 with no recorded benefit), but nothing here shows derate occurring below the published operating envelope, and the affected serials (2419B, 2420B, 2426B, 2427C, 2428C, 2436C) overlap the same bands as non-derating control units (KVP36-2420B-0350, KVP36-2420B-0355, KVP36-2421B-0201). Impact is small and bounded — partial afternoon curtailment on 6 of 376 units over roughly two years, 28.5 labour hours total, no outages and no hard trips — so this does not warrant commercial action now.
response.contradicting_evidence: Three signals argue for a real model defect rather than designed behaviour: KVP36-2419B-0361 recurred across two separate seasons (WO-2024-00163, WO-2025-00688); parts were consumed with no recorded improvement (cooling fan x3 in WO-2025-00908, air filter set in WO-2026-00571); and every OEM case remains pending (WO-2025-00688, WO-2025-00908, WO-2026-00571, WO-2026-00586) rather than closed as normal operation. A same-model unit also logged unexplained low airflow with clean filters and all fans running (WO-2025-00920), hinting at a cooling-control issue the current data cannot resolve. If Kelvara confirms the derate setpoint activates below the published ambient envelope, this flips to a warranty-grade H1 finding.
